# sitesolide

> sitesolide deploys small software, static sites and apps in any language, to one Debian server its owner runs: `sitesolide deploy` in a folder puts it live on HTTPS, restricted when private, open only to the people given access, with secrets held on the server and set from its dashboard. There is no staging: a real deploy is live for every visitor at once.

This file is for an agent (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor) that uses the `sitesolide` CLI or its MCP server on a user's behalf. `sitesolide --help` prints every command; the links below are the reference.

**Is it installed and set up?**

- `sitesolide --version --json` ends with a `result` carrying `version`. If the command is missing, the user installs it: `curl -fsSL https://github.com/cthiriet/sitesolide/releases/latest/download/install.sh | sh` (one binary in `~/.local/bin`, no Bun needed).
- `sitesolide status --json`, from any folder, says which mode the workstation is in and whether it works:
  - a `result` with `projects`, `ports` and `memory`: the owner's workstation, which reaches the server over SSH;
  - a `result` with `api`, `identity` and `projects`: a workstation with a token, which goes through the dashboard's API;
  - an `error` whose message starts `missing settings:`: nothing is configured. A new server is `machine` then `setup` (below); a server already installed is `sitesolide init --server <user@host> --zone <dns.zone> --email <address>`; someone with a token runs `sitesolide login`. Never guess a server or a zone;
  - any other `error`: follow its `hint`.
- The configuration is `~/.config/sitesolide/config.json` (`server`, `zone`, `email`; `api` with a token), or `$SITESOLIDE_CONFIG_DIR/config.json` for a second installation. The `secrets/` folder beside it holds the workstation's credentials: never read it.

**Deploying a folder.**

1. `sitesolide detect --json` (MCP `detect`): an `inferred` event, then a `result` with `kind`, `manifest`, `reasons`, `notes`, `written`. It reads no server and writes nothing. The `notes` name the secrets the code reads and the network calls it makes.
2. Review the manifest and the notes with the user, who decides `"network": "outbound"` (without it a service reaches only the loopback, DNS included), `"secrets": ["<slug>.env"]` (a project declares `<slug>.env` and `<slug>-<name>` files alone, never another project's or the machine's), a service's `backup` command when it runs a server database in the data folder (PostgreSQL, MongoDB: the hourly snapshot refuses one without it), and the slug, which is the address `https://<slug>.<zone>/`. `sitesolide detect --write` writes `sitesolide.json`, never over an existing one; `--slug <name>` names the project otherwise than after its folder. Every key: docs/manifest.md.
3. `sitesolide deploy --dry-run --json` (MCP `deploy` with `dry_run: true`): reads the server, shows the systemd unit and Caddy block an app would get as `file` events and every action as `planned`, changes nothing, and does not run the build. Show the user what it plans.
4. Once the user agrees: `sitesolide deploy --json`. In a folder still without a manifest, `sitesolide deploy --yes --json` (MCP `accept_inferred: true`) writes the inferred one and deploys; it is refused when the server already has a project of that name: pick another `--slug`, never deploy over it.
5. Read the last line. A `result` carries `slug`, `kind` (`static`, `service`, `services`), `port`, `url` and, over SSH, `status`, the HTTP status of the final check: give the user the `url`. `manifestWritten: true` means `sitesolide.json` changed on disk (an inferred manifest, a port chosen, general access set from the dashboard): commit it. An `error` carries a `hint`: follow it.
6. A failed restart, or a site answering 500 or 502: `sitesolide logs --json --lines 100` (MCP `logs`), one `log` event per entry with `at`, `unit`, `priority`, `message`; priority 3 and below are errors. Fix the code, deploy again.

An app without `port` gets the lowest free one between 3000 and 3099 from `deploy`, written back into `sitesolide.json`. A port taken: delete `port` and deploy again.

**Background work.** `detect` infers web servers and static sites only; a process that is not one goes under `services`, by hand, never as the top-level `start`, which is always a server. A worker, `{ "start": "...", "internal": true }` with no `port`, runs for good, listens on nothing and is restarted with growing delays when it falls; it should exit cleanly on SIGTERM. A scheduled service, `{ "start": "...", "schedule": "*:0/15", "timeout": "15m" }`, runs to its end at the times a systemd calendar expression names (`hourly`, `daily`, `Mon..Fri 08:00`, `*-*-* 06:30 Europe/Paris`), `timeout` 1h by default and 24h at most, with no `port`, `routes` or `backup`; a deployment does not run it. `cpu` (`50%` is half a core) caps a service, or every one at the top level. A project of workers and scheduled services alone, without `publicDir`, serves no page: its address answers a line saying so, and `domain` is refused. `deploy` stops on a schedule systemd on the machine does not read, and fails when a server or worker falls within ten seconds of its restart: read `logs`. A headless browser, heavy computing and mass email from the machine's own address do not belong on the machine that serves every site: tell the user before writing one (docs/manifest.md, "What fits on the machine").

**The `--json` contract.** Every command but `init` and `run` takes `--json`. Standard output then carries one JSON object per line and nothing else, and the run ends with exactly one `result` (`ok: true`, `command`, the command's data) or one `error` (`message`, `details`, `hint`), always the last line; a failure exits non-zero. Before it: `step`, `info`, `planned` (`message`); `warning` (`message`, `details`), to relay to the user; `output` (`stream`, `line`), a line of the build, rsync or a script; `file` (`name`, `content`); `inferred`; `log`; `check` (`step`, `status` among `done`, `ok`, `skip`, `todo`, `fail`, `title`, `detail`), one line of setup's or upgrade's checklist. Under `--json` nothing prompts and ssh never asks: the key must be loaded (`ssh-add`) and the host key already known, or the connection fails at once. Every command's `result` fields: docs/agents.md.

**MCP.** `sitesolide mcp` serves the CLI as tools over stdio, with no configuration of its own; each tool runs the command with `--json` in the folder named, an absolute path, and returns its events.

| Tool | Arguments | Changes |
|---|---|---|
| `detect` | `folder`, `slug` | nothing, reads no server |
| `deploy` | `folder`, `dry_run`, `accept_inferred`, `slug` | the live site, unless `dry_run` |
| `status` | | nothing |
| `logs` | `folder`, `lines` | nothing |
| `access` | `folder` | nothing |
| `share` | `folder`, `who`, `role`, `expires`, `remove` | who may open the app and its data; from Viewer up, who sees or changes the project in the dashboard |
| `lock_status` | `folder` | nothing, never shows the code |

Register it in Claude Code with `claude mcp add --scope user --transport stdio sitesolide -- sitesolide mcp`; any other client launches the command `sitesolide` with the argument `mcp`. Keep `deploy` and `share` on "ask". `remove`, `lock`, `unlock`, `domain --activate`, `setup`, `upgrade`, `refresh` and `--force` are not tools, on purpose: they stay the owner's.

**With a token.** A workstation or sandbox without SSH to the server deploys with a personal token, `sst_` then 43 characters, which the owner creates on the dashboard's Tokens page, or someone who signs in to the dashboard mints there for themselves, never stronger than their roles. The user hands it over without pasting it into the conversation: `SITESOLIDE_API=https://dashboard.<zone>` and `SITESOLIDE_TOKEN` in the agent's environment, both together, which win over the files and need nothing kept on disk, or `sitesolide login --url https://dashboard.<zone> --token-stdin` with the token piped in, which checks it and keeps it in `~/.config/sitesolide/secrets/team-token`, 0600, with the address beside it. The token `login` kept goes to that address alone: a `SITESOLIDE_API` or a `config.json` naming another dashboard is refused `unauthenticated`; never point either elsewhere. Then `deploy`, `status`, `logs` (`--lines` up to 500), `share`, `secrets` and `restart` run through the dashboard, and `detect` as anywhere; the owner's commands (`lock`, `unlock`, `domain`, `remove`, `run`, `people`, `refresh`) are refused with `needs-ssh`. `deploy` takes no option there: no `--dry-run` (review `sitesolide.json` with the user instead; the dashboard judges the manifest before anything is built or sent) and no `--yes` (write the manifest first with `sitesolide detect --write`). A token's new projects are Restricted unless the token may deploy public sites, and what its scope does not allow, or for a person's own token what their role no longer allows, is refused with `out-of-scope`: never work around it with another slug or token. `--api` sends an owner's command through the API too.

**Secrets and restarts with a token.** With a token minted with Manage secrets, `sitesolide secrets --json` lists the project's secret files and their variable names (`secrets.files`, each `name`, `variables`, `restartPending`, `writable`), never a value: no route reads one back; a token without it is refused `out-of-scope`. Such a token changes `<slug>.env` alone, once the deployed manifest declares it: `sitesolide secrets set NAME --stdin --json` reads the value from standard input, one trailing line break dropped, and `sitesolide secrets remove NAME... --json` takes variables out; `--restart` restarts the service after the change. `secrets set` is for the user to run in their own terminal, typing the value at its prompt, or for a value the agent generates itself and pipes, `openssl rand -hex 32 | sitesolide secrets set SESSION_SECRET --stdin --json`; never a value read from the conversation, the repository or a message, and never `NAME=value` or a value as an argument, which is refused before anything is sent. A name that looks like a value, over 64 characters or starting like a service's key, is refused `looks-like-value`, never quoted: tell the user it may be in the shell's history and to change it at its source. Under `--json`, `set` never prompts and needs `--stdin`. `unconfirmed` means the change was sent and no answer came: check with `sitesolide secrets --json`, then run the same command once more, never in a loop. `sitesolide restart --json`, which any token that deploys the project may run, restarts its service and ends in an `error` unless it holds: read `logs` then. There is no MCP tool for secrets, on purpose.

**Access.** A restricted site opens to its people with access alone: per project, entries of an email or a whole domain written `@acme.com`, each with a role, `can-open` (Can open), `viewer`, `developer` or `admin`, each including the ones below it. Can open opens the site; Viewer also sees the project in the dashboard, Developer deploys and writes secrets, Admin looks after all of it.

- `sitesolide share --json` (MCP `access`) reads the general access (`public`, `restricted`, `code`), the `entries` and the `message` to send after giving someone access.
- `sitesolide share alice@example.com --json` gives Can open; `--role viewer|developer|admin` another role, `@example.com` everyone at that domain (Can open only); `--remove <email|@domain>` takes access away from their next request. The `result` carries `entries` and `changes` (each `who`, `change`, `role`).
- Someone outside the company's domains gets password access, Can open only: the password comes back once, in `changes`, for the user to send; `--expires 24h|7d|30d|never`, 7d by default. Never store or repeat it.
- Access gives real people the app and its data. Ask the user who should get in and with which role, give it to exactly the addresses or the domain they named and nobody else, tell them who will get in and wait for their yes. Give them the result's `message` to send.
- In the dashboard, a site's Access section shows the same, general access first, then its people with access; the owner's People page lists everyone across projects. Both are the user's, not an agent's.
- Never make a site Public: general access is the dashboard's. With a token, `share` gives Can open alone, to people of the company's domains or one of those domains, never password access; anything more is `out-of-scope`, for the user to give from the dashboard.

**A new server.** Run these only when the user asked for a server; the tokens are theirs.

- `sitesolide machine create --provider <provider> --name <name> --json` orders a Debian 13 VM from `hetzner`, `digitalocean`, `aws`, `gcp`, `azure`, `vultr`, `linode` or `scaleway` (each provider's cheapest current type with 2 GB in Europe unless `--type`, `--location`) with a firewall opening 22, 80, 443 and ICMP and the workstation's SSH key, then waits until SSH lets its account in. The `result` carries `machine` and `next`, the `setup` command to run, which names the account the image lets in (`root`, or a sudoer such as AWS's `admin`, with `--user deploy`). `sitesolide machine providers --json` says which providers have credentials on this workstation and where they come from. Credentials come from the provider's environment variables, standard input with `--token-stdin`, or the provider's own CLI already signed in, never an option. `sitesolide machine list --provider <provider> --json` lists what sitesolide created. An interrupted run is finished by running the same command again. `sitesolide setup` alone at a terminal is an interactive wizard for a person: an agent never runs it bare, it runs `machine create` then `setup` with its options.
- `sitesolide setup root@<ipv4> --zone <dns.zone> --email <address> --json` hardens the machine, creates the DNS records through the provider `--dns` names (`cloudflare` by default, `route53`, `azure-dns`, `digitalocean-dns`, `hetzner-dns`, `scaleway-dns`, `vultr-dns`, `linode-dns`, `ovh`, `gandi`, `porkbun`; `manual` when the records are made by hand and each name gets its own certificate), installs every component and writes the configuration. It is idempotent and resumable: on an installed machine it changes nothing, after a failure it resumes at the failed step. `--dry-run` checks every step and changes nothing. The DNS credentials come from the provider's variables (`CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN`, `SITESOLIDE_DNS_<...>` for the others, see docs/dns/) or standard input with `--dns-credentials-stdin`; under `--json` it never prompts. They are laid on the machine for Caddy: they must be scoped to the zone, and an agent never reuses a cloud's broad token for them.
- The run that draws the dashboard's and the portal's passwords prints them once on standard error, for the user, never in an event: never repeat, store or use them.
- A configuration that names another server, zone or account stops setup; it may point at a machine in service. A second installation gets `--config-dir <dir>` on setup, then `SITESOLIDE_CONFIG_DIR=<dir>` before every command.
- `sitesolide upgrade --dry-run --json` reads the configured machine and lists every component the CLI's release would change, each `up-to-date`, `out-of-date` or `missing`, changing nothing. `sitesolide upgrade --json` redeploys only the components found out of date, live, so only when the user asked; it never installs a missing one (`setup` does, the `result` carries the command in `next`), never reads a secret, and resumes at the failed component when run again.
- `sitesolide refresh --all --dry-run --json` reads every project's manifest on the server and lists the units this release would write again, each project `outdated`, `current`, `kept` (a unit edited by hand, never replaced), `refused` or `static`, changing nothing. `sitesolide refresh --all --json` writes those units, without sending any code, and restarts and checks each project's services, live, one project at a time, stopping at the first that does not hold: only when the user asked, after an upgrade whose notes say the generated units changed. `refresh <slug>` does one project.

**Rules an agent never breaks.**

- Secrets never go into the repository, `sitesolide.json`, `env`, a command-line argument or the conversation. The user sets them in the dashboard's Secrets section, `https://dashboard.<zone>`, or, with a token that may manage secrets, runs `sitesolide secrets set NAME` themselves and types the value at its prompt; an agent pipes to `sitesolide secrets set NAME --stdin` only a value it generated itself, never one from the conversation. A deploy missing one stops before the restart and names the page: tell the user, deploy again once they have. Never read, print or guess a secret, nor ask the user to paste one. Tokens, a cloud provider's, Cloudflare's or a sitesolide token, reach the CLI through environment variables or standard input only.
- Never change the server by hand: no `ssh`, `sudo`, `systemctl` or file edits there; everything goes through the CLI or the MCP tools. Never `caddy stop` or `caddy start`: they talk to the Caddy in service whatever `--config` says, and a stop takes every site down.
- Only on the user's explicit decision, never on your own: `upgrade` and `refresh` (their `--dry-run` only reads), `--force` over a file edited on the machine, `setup --dns-replace` over records that point elsewhere, `setup --any-os`, `machine destroy --confirm <name>` (the disk and the provider's backups go with it), `remove --confirm <slug>` (what changed since the last backup is lost), `lock`, `unlock`, `domain --activate` or `--deactivate`, and giving access to anyone, or a role, the user did not name.
- Every `error` carries a `hint`: follow it, and never answer a refusal with `--force` or a workaround. A refused or dropped SSH connection during setup is most likely a fail2ban ban of this workstation: never retry in a loop; wait the 10 minutes it lasts, then run the same command once.
- What is deployed is live at once: dry-run first, show the user, and deploy on their yes.
